_readme: Cross-language conformance fixture for the tab-title cleaning rule.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS: every writer of a tab title cleans it -- the worker at the three
title-writing RPCs (OpenAgent, RenameAgent, UpdateTerminalTitle) and at the plan
auto-rename, and the browser at the inline rename it sends them. No path refuses a
title. That only holds if the two implementations clean IDENTICALLY: the browser
patches its own tab metadata optimistically, so a rule that drifts leaves the tab strip
showing one title while the worker stores another, with no error anywhere to say so.
This file is the check: both suites read it, so EDITING ONE SIDE WITHOUT THE OTHER IS
THE EXACT BUG IT PREVENTS -- the language that drifts is the one whose CI turns red.
THE RULE, in order: cut to 128 UTF-8 BYTES at a character boundary, strip the forbidden
characters (the control blocks, U+FEFF, and the four templating characters), then trim
the whitespace at both ends. The order is load-bearing. The strip only REMOVES bytes,
so a cut string still fits the limit -- which is what makes the rule total (it has
nothing to refuse) and idempotent. The 'strip runs after the cut' case below is the one
input where the reverse order answers differently, and it is pinned deliberately.
The unit is BYTES on both sides, because Go's `len` counts bytes. 128 bytes is 128
ASCII characters but only 42 CJK characters, so a character count and a byte count
disagree on every wider script -- the '50 CJK characters' case is 50 characters and 150
bytes. The cut also has to land on a character boundary in both languages:
String.prototype.slice counts UTF-16 code units and splits a surrogate pair in half, so
the 'cut lands inside a surrogate pair' case is what refuses that shortcut.
CONSUMED BY (keep both in sync with this schema):
Go: backend/util/validate/name_test.go   TestCleanNameConformance
TS: frontend/src/lib/validate.test.ts    cleanName conformance block
THE CONTRACT, per case: `input` and `cleaned` are both SPECS, and a spec builds one
string as `text` repeated `repeat` times followed by `tail` (`repeat` defaults to 1;
`text` and `tail` default to the empty string). The spec exists so a boundary reads as
the NUMBER 128 rather than as 128 characters a reader has to count. Both sides assert:
clean(build(input))   == build(cleaned)
clean(build(cleaned)) == build(cleaned)   -- idempotence, for every case
`why` is documentation only; neither suite asserts on it.
Every character outside printable ASCII is written as an escape, so this file states
which code point each case means and stays readable in a diff.

cases.why: an already clean title passes through unchanged
an empty title cleans to empty -- each caller supplies its own fallback
the whitespace at both ends is trimmed
a C0 control character (NUL) is stripped and the rest of the title survives
the C1 block is control too: Go's unicode.IsControl covers U+0080-U+009F, so the browser regex has to cover it as well
each of the four templating characters is stripped: double quote, backslash, dollar, percent

a LEADING U+FEFF is stripped. JS trim() removes it and Go TrimSpace keeps it, so a pasted byte order mark was the one input on which the two rules disagreed. This case pins the Go half, where the strip is what removes it
a U+FEFF in the MIDDLE is stripped too. No trim reaches it on either side, so this case pins BOTH halves: the character rule has to name U+FEFF, not lean on the trim
a title of forbidden characters and whitespace cleans to EMPTY -- the caller's fallback case
exactly 128 bytes: the limit is inclusive, so nothing is cut
129 bytes: one byte over, so one byte goes
50 CJK characters is 150 bytes: under a 128-CHARACTER cap and over the 128-BYTE one. The cut at byte 128 lands inside the 43rd character, so it moves back to 126 bytes
32 emoji is exactly 128 bytes (4 each): an astral character that sits on the limit is kept whole

the cut lands inside a surrogate pair: 30 units of 5 bytes is 150 bytes, and byte 128 sits in the 26th emoji, so the whole emoji goes and 126 bytes remain. A UTF-16 slice(0,128) keeps half a pair here
the cut leaves a trailing space, which the trim then removes -- the trim runs AFTER the cut
the strip runs after the cut: the first 128 bytes are all stripped, so nothing survives. The reverse order would have kept the two letters, and this case pins the order the rule chose
120 bytes of CJK plus a stripped character: under the limit, so the strip alone applies
